questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
questions.title: == vs .equals() in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`==`** compares **references** (memory addresses) for objects and raw **values** for primitives, while **`.equals()`** compares the **logical content** of objects. For Strings, `==` can deceptively return `true` because identical literals share one object in the **String pool**, so always use `.equals()` for content comparison.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands reference vs value comparison and knows that == on Strings is unreliable because of String pool sharing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare String content and getting false negatives on data from forms, files, or databases, or assuming == always compares values
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that string literals share references in the pool, making == accidentally pass in tests but fail in production — and use the null-safe "literal".equals(var) pattern

sections.title: Reference vs Value Comparison in Java
sections.content:
Java has two different comparison mechanisms, and mixing them up causes bugs that compile fine but fail at runtime. The **`==` operator** compares what is stored in the variable itself. For **primitives** (`int`, `double`, `boolean`), that is the actual value. For **objects** (`String`, `Integer`, custom classes), that is the memory address — the reference pointing to where the object lives on the heap. The **`.equals()` method** compares the logical content inside objects.

Comparing two houses: `==` asks "are these the exact same house at the same address?" while `.equals()` asks "do these houses have the same layout inside?" For `String` this matters because Java stores string literals in a **String pool** — a shared area where identical literals reuse the same object. That makes `==` accidentally work sometimes, which trains bad habits.

sections.title: == vs .equals() at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|== operator|~Compares the variable's slot|primitives: actual value|objects: memory address|fast, but not content
blue|.equals()|~Compares logical content|Object default = ==|override for value equality|String/Integer override it
emerald|String pool|~Literals share one object|"hi" == "hi" is true|new String("hi") is false|why == feels like it works
rose|Safe habit|~Use .equals() for content|null-safe: "x".equals(v)|== only for primitives/enums|enums are singletons

sections.title: The Practical Difference
sections.content:
| Aspect | `==` | `.equals()` |
|---|---|---|
| Compares | Reference (or primitive value) | Logical content |
| Works on | Primitives + objects | Objects only |
| String literals | `true` (shared pool) | `true` |
| `new String("x")` | `false` (new object) | `true` |
| Null-safe | Yes (`a == null`) | No (NPE if left side is null) |

sections.title: Wrong — == on Strings from runtime sources
Right — .equals() compares content (null-safe form)
When to Use Each Comparison
sections.content:
Use **`==` for primitives** (`int`, `double`, `boolean`, `char`) — it compares actual values and primitives have no `.equals()`.

Use **`==` for null checks** (`if (obj == null)`) — calling `.equals()` on `null` throws `NullPointerException`.

Use **`==` for enum comparisons** — enum constants are singletons, so reference equality is correct and fast.

Use **`.equals()` for all object content comparison** — `String`, `Integer`, and custom classes where you care about logical equality. Never use `==` for String content in production code.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `==` for String comparison on user input**: `if (userName == "admin")` fails because input creates new String objects, not pool references. Always use `.equals()` for strings from external sources.
- **Forgetting null checks before `.equals()`**: `userName.equals("admin")` throws `NullPointerException` when `userName` is `null`. Use `"admin".equals(userName)` to stay safe.
- **Assuming `==` works because tests passed**: literals in test code share pool references, so `==` accidentally passes, but production data from databases or APIs creates new objects where `==` fails.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`==` on primitives** — compares actual values (`5 == 5` is `true`).
- **`==` on objects** — compares memory addresses, not content.
- **String pool** — identical literals share one object, so `==` can deceptively pass.
- **`.equals()`** — compares logical content; override it in custom classes.
- **Null-safe habit** — write `"literal".equals(var)` to dodge `NullPointerException`.
- **Use `==` for enums** — they're singletons, so reference equality is correct.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The double equals operator compares references for objects and values for primitives, while dot equals compares the logical content inside objects. Here's the key distinction: when you use double equals on two String variables, it checks if they point to the exact same object in memory. When you use dot equals, it checks if the strings contain the same sequence of characters. This matters because Java has something called the String pool. When you write String x equals quote hello quote, Java stores that literal in a special memory area. If you write String y equals quote hello quote later, Java reuses the same object from the pool, so x double equals y returns true. But if you get a string from user input or a database, it's a new object. So even if the content is hello, double equals returns false because they're different objects in memory. That's why you should always use dot equals for strings. One pitfall freshers hit is writing if username double equals quote admin quote for login checks. This works in unit tests with string literals, but fails in production when username comes from a form submission. The safe pattern is to put the known string first, like if quote admin quote dot equals username, which also avoids null pointer exceptions if username is null.

questions.question: What is the ternary operator in Java and how is it different from if-else?
questions.title: Ternary Operator in Java
questions.direct_answer: The **ternary operator** `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` is Java's only three-operand operator and is an **expression** that produces a value, unlike `if-else` which is a **statement**. Because it returns a value, you can use it inline in assignments, method arguments, and return statements. Keep it to simple one-line binary choices — nest it and readability collapses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the expression-versus-statement distinction and when concise conditional syntax helps versus hurts readability
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Nesting ternary operators deeply into unreadable code, or trying to use the ternary to execute actions rather than produce a value
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the ternary is an expression you can drop inline, while if-else is a statement that executes blocks and can't be assigned

sections.title: The Ternary Operator as a Value-Producing Expression
sections.content:
The **ternary operator** (or conditional operator) is Java's only three-operand operator: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`. The critical point is that it is an **expression**, not a **statement**. An expression produces a value; a statement executes an action. So you can use the ternary anywhere a value is expected: variable assignments, method arguments, return statements, or inside other expressions.

It is a compact `if-else` that collapses to a single value. `String status = isActive ? "Online" : "Offline"` assigns one of two strings without four lines of `if-else`. Reach for it on simple binary choices that produce a value. The rule of thumb: if it needs more than one line or the condition isn't obvious, use `if-else` instead.

sections.title: Ternary at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Ternary|~One-line value chooser|cond ? a : b|returns a value|three operands
blue|Expression vs statement|~Ternary returns a value|if-else runs blocks|use inline in assignments|if-else can't be assigned
emerald|Best fit|~Simple binary choice|default values|name != null ? name : "Guest"|fits on one line
rose|Avoid|~Nested ternaries|hard to read|no side-effect actions|wrap in ( ) inside concatenation

sections.title: Practical Ternary Operator Usage
When to Choose Ternary Over If-Else
sections.content:
Use the **ternary for simple binary decisions** that produce a value: setting a variable, returning from a method, or passing an argument that fits on one line.

Use it for **default value patterns**: `String name = input != null ? input : "default"` is clearer than four lines of `if-else`.

Use it in **initialization**: `final int max = useCache ? CACHE_MAX : DB_MAX` keeps the variable immutable with conditional logic.

Avoid it when **conditions are complex** (multiple ANDs/ORs), when **actions need multiple statements**, or when **nesting more than once**. If the line exceeds about 80 characters, refactor to `if-else`.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Nesting ternaries deeply**: `x = a ? b ? c : d : e ? f : g` is unreadable. Limit to one level of nesting.
- **Using ternary for actions instead of values**: `x > 0 ? doSomething() : doOtherThing()` compiles but misuses the operator — it is for producing values, not side effects. Use `if-else` for actions.
- **Forgetting parentheses in concatenation**: `"Result: " + x > 0 ? "pos" : "neg"` parses wrong due to precedence. Wrap it: `"Result: " + (x > 0 ? "pos" : "neg")`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Syntax** — `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` returns one of two values.
- **Expression vs statement** — the ternary returns a value; `if-else` executes blocks.
- **Inline usage** — works in assignments, method calls, returns, and concatenation.
- **Readability rule** — simple one-line choices only; switch to `if-else` for complex logic.
- **Type compatibility** — both branches must be types Java can unify.
- **Null-safe fallback** — `name != null ? name : "default"` is the idiomatic default pattern.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The ternary operator is a compact way to choose between two values based on a condition. The syntax is condition question mark valueIfTrue colon valueIfFalse. The key difference from if-else is that the ternary operator is an expression that produces a value, so you can use it directly in assignments, method arguments, or return statements. For example, String status equals isActive question mark quote online quote colon quote offline quote assigns one of two strings in a single line, whereas if-else would take four lines and you'd have to declare status before the if block. The ternary operator is perfect for simple binary decisions like setting default values: String name equals input not equals null question mark input colon quote guest quote. It's clean and readable when it fits on one line. The mistake freshers make is overusing it by nesting ternary operators deeply. If you write something like x equals a question mark b question mark c colon d colon e, it becomes unreadable fast. Another pitfall is trying to use ternary for actions instead of values. The ternary operator is designed to produce a value, not execute code with side effects. If you need to run multiple statements or the logic is complex, just use if-else. The rule I follow is if it doesn't fit clearly on one line, switch to if-else for maintainability.

When is it better to use if-else instead of the ternary operator?

questions.question: What is the difference between pre-increment (++i) and post-increment (i++) in Java?
questions.title: Pre-increment vs Post-increment in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Pre-increment `++i`** adds 1 first and then returns the **new** value; **post-increment `i++`** returns the **current** value first and then adds 1. The difference only shows up when the expression's value is used in an assignment or calculation — as standalone statements they are identical.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of expression evaluation order and operator side effects, usually probed with tricky output-prediction questions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking ++i and i++ always differ, or expecting int b = i++ to give b the incremented value
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through a compound expression like int b = ++i + i++ step by step, showing what each operator returns and when i changes

sections.title: Pre-increment vs Post-increment Evaluation Order
sections.content:
Increment operators modify a variable and return a value, but the timing differs. **Pre-increment `++i`** follows "increment first, use later": it adds 1 to the variable, then returns the new value to the expression. **Post-increment `i++`** follows "use first, increment later": it returns the current value to the expression, then adds 1. In a standalone statement like `i++;` or `++i;` on its own line there is no difference — both just add 1.

The distinction only emerges when you use the operator's return value in an assignment, method call, or calculation. Pre-increment is "prepare then present"; post-increment is "present then prepare." Interviewers test this to see whether you understand operator side effects and evaluation order.

sections.title: ++i vs i++ at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|++i (pre)|~Increment, then read|i becomes i+1 first|returns the new value|prepare then present
blue|i++ (post)|~Read, then increment|returns the old value|i becomes i+1 after|present then prepare
emerald|Standalone|~Same effect|i++; equals ++i;|both add 1|no value is used
rose|In expressions|~Values differ|int b = ++i vs i++|array[i++] is common|avoid chaining ++ in one line

sections.title: Pre-increment vs Post-increment Behavior
sections.content:
| Aspect | Pre-increment (`++i`) | Post-increment (`i++`) |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluation order | Increment first, return new value | Return current value, increment after |
| Standalone usage | `i` becomes `i+1` | `i` becomes `i+1` (identical) |
| In assignment | `int b = ++i` assigns incremented value | `int b = i++` assigns original value |
| Expression value | New value after increment | Old value before increment |
| Memory ops | Read, increment, write, return new | Read, return old, increment, write |

sections.title: Wrong assumption — post-increment returns the old value
sections.content:
```java
int i = 5;
int b = i++;            // fresher expects b == 6
System.out.println(b);  // 5 — post-increment returns the OLD value
System.out.println(i);  // 6 — i was incremented afterwards
```

sections.title: Right — pre-increment returns the new value
sections.content:
```java
int i = 5;
int b = ++i;            // increment first, then return
System.out.println(b);  // 6 — new value returned
System.out.println(i);  // 6
```
For the classic trap `int b = ++i + i++` with `i = 5`: `++i` makes `i = 6` and yields 6, then `i++` yields 6 and makes `i = 7`, so `b = 12` and `i = 7`.

sections.title: When to Use Each Operator
sections.content:
Use **pre-increment `++i`** in for-loops where the increment value doesn't matter — modern JVMs optimize both identically, so this is a style choice.

Use it when you want the incremented value immediately, like `return ++counter` for a sequence generator.

Use **post-increment `i++`** when you need the original value before incrementing, such as `array[index++]` — use the current index, then advance.

In practice, **avoid increment operators inside complex expressions**. Write `i = i + 1` separately for clarity; expressions like `x = i++ + ++i` are interview gotchas, not production code.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Chaining increments in expressions**: `int result = ++i + i++ + i` is unreadable. Break it into separate statements.
- **Expecting both to behave the same in assignments**: `int b = i++` gives `b` the old value; only `i` is incremented.
- **Post-increment in return statements**: `return count++` returns the current value, then increments — the caller gets the old value, often not what's intended.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`++i` (pre)** — increments first, then returns the new value.
- **`i++` (post)** — returns the current value, then increments.
- **Standalone** — `++i` and `i++` are identical when used alone on a line.
- **In expressions** — the difference only matters when the return value is used.
- **For-loops** — `i++` is convention, but `++i` works identically.
- **Readability** — avoid multiple increments in one expression; clarity beats cleverness.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Pre-increment with plus plus i increments the variable first, then returns the new value. Post-increment with i plus plus returns the current value first, then increments the variable. The easiest way to see the difference is with an assignment. If i is 5 and you write int b equals plus plus i, it increments i to 6, then assigns 6 to b. But if you write int b equals i plus plus, it assigns the current value 5 to b, then increments i to 6. So b ends up with different values depending on which operator you used. In a standalone statement like just i plus plus on its own line, there's no difference. Both just add 1 to i. The distinction only matters when you're using the operator's return value in an assignment or calculation. In for-loops, most people write i plus plus out of habit, but plus plus i works exactly the same because we're not using the return value, we just want the side effect of incrementing. One common mistake freshers make is thinking these operators always behave differently, even in standalone statements. Another is writing complex expressions like int b equals plus plus i plus i plus plus, which is technically valid but terrible for readability. In professional code, keep it simple and use these operators in predictable ways.

questions.question: What is short-circuit evaluation in Java and how do && and || use it?
questions.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation with && and || in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Short-circuit evaluation** means Java stops evaluating a boolean expression as soon as the result is certain: with **`&&`**, a `false` left side skips the right; with **`||`**, a `true` left side skips the right. This is both a performance optimization and the standard **null-safety** pattern, e.g. `obj != null && obj.isValid()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows logical operators have execution-order implications beyond boolean logic, especially for null-safety guards
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming both sides of && or || always execute, leading to NullPointerExceptions or side effects that silently never run
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the null-safety pattern obj != null && obj.getName().equals("foo") and explain why order matters because evaluation is left-to-right

sections.title: How Short-Circuit Evaluation Protects Your Code
sections.content:
**Short-circuit evaluation** is Java's behavior where logical operators stop evaluating as soon as the outcome is certain. With **`&&` (AND)**, if the left operand is `false`, the whole expression is `false` — the right side is skipped. With **`||` (OR)**, if the left operand is `true`, the whole expression is `true` — again the right side is skipped. This is not just performance; it is a safety mechanism.

It works like a checkpoint: if the first guard rejects you, there is no point sending you to the second. The most powerful use is **null safety**: `if (user != null && user.isActive())` works because if `user` is `null`, Java never calls `user.isActive()`, avoiding a `NullPointerException`. The non-short-circuit operators `&` and `|` always evaluate both sides and are almost never used with booleans.

sections.title: Short-Circuit Logic at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|AND (&&)|~Stops on false|false and anything is false|right side skipped|guards the right side
blue|OR|~Stops on true|true or anything is true|right side skipped|early exit
emerald|Null safety|~Check before use|obj != null && obj.m()|order matters|evaluated left-to-right
rose|Bitwise & and pipe|~No skipping|both sides always run|risk of NPE or side effects|rarely used on booleans

sections.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation in Action
Wrong — null check placed after the method call
Right — null check first lets && short-circuit
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Relying on a side effect in the right operand**: `if (false && counter++ > 0)` never runs `counter++`. If you need the side effect, run it separately.
- **Wrong order in null checks**: `if (user.getName() != null && user != null)` crashes because Java calls `getName()` on `null` before checking `user`. Null check first, always.
- **Using `&` or `|` by mistake**: `if (obj != null & obj.isValid())` uses bitwise AND, evaluates both sides, and throws `NullPointerException`. Use `&&` and `||` for boolean logic.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`&&`** — stops on a `false` left side; `false && anything` is `false`.
- **`||`** — stops on a `true` left side; `true || anything` is `true`.
- **Null safety** — `obj != null && obj.method()` prevents `NullPointerException`.
- **Performance** — expensive right-side work is skipped when the left side decides.
- **`&` and `|`** — bitwise operators that always evaluate both sides.
- **Order matters** — Java evaluates left-to-right, so guards go on the left.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Short-circuit evaluation means Java stops checking a logical expression as soon as it knows the answer. For double ampersand, if the left side is false, Java doesn't bother evaluating the right side because false and anything is always false. For double pipe, if the left side is true, the right side is skipped because true or anything is always true. This is incredibly useful for null safety. The classic pattern is if obj not equals null double ampersand obj dot method. If obj is null, the first check fails, so Java never tries to call the method, which would throw a null pointer exception. It's like a guard clause that protects the rest of the expression. Another practical use is performance: if you have an expensive database check on the right side, you can put a cheap cache check on the left with double ampersand, and the database is only hit if the cache misses. One mistake freshers make is relying on side effects on the right side. If you write if false double ampersand counter plus plus, the counter never increments because short-circuit skips it. Another mistake is getting the order wrong: if you write user dot getName not equals null double ampersand user not equals null, it crashes on null users because you're calling getName before checking if user is null. Always put the null check first.

questions.question: What are bitwise operators in Java and give a practical example of when to use them?
questions.title: Bitwise Operators in Java — Practical Use Cases
questions.direct_answer: **Bitwise operators** work on the individual bits of integers: `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `~` (NOT), `<<` (left shift), `>>` (signed right shift), and `>>>` (unsigned right shift). Common practical uses are checking even/odd with `n & 1`, multiplying or dividing by powers of two with shifts, and packing boolean flags into one int for compact permissions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of low-level bit operations and the ability to name a real use case such as flag/permission masks or even-odd checks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing bitwise & with logical &&, or memorizing the operators without any real-world application
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show concrete examples: n & 1 for even/odd without modulo, n << 1 to multiply by 2, and bit flags for compact permission storage

sections.title: Understanding Bitwise Operations and Their Practical Value
sections.content:
**Bitwise operators** work on the individual bits of integer types (`int`, `long`, `byte`, `short`), treating numbers as sequences of 0s and 1s. Java has seven: **`&` (AND)** outputs 1 only if both bits are 1, **`|` (OR)** outputs 1 if either bit is 1, **`^` (XOR)** outputs 1 if the bits differ, **`~` (NOT)** flips all bits, **`<<` (left shift)** shifts left filling zeros, **`>>` (signed right shift)** shifts right preserving the sign, and **`>>>` (unsigned right shift)** shifts right filling zeros.

The most common real use is **bit flags for permissions**: instead of four boolean fields, pack them into one int using powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8) and use bitwise ops to set or check them. Bitwise is also handy for even/odd checks (`n & 1`) and multiplying by powers of two (`n << 3` multiplies by 8).

sections.title: Bitwise Operators at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|AND (&)|~1 only if both bits 1|test a flag: x & FLAG|n & 1 gives even/odd|mask out bits
blue|OR (pipe)|~1 if either bit 1|combine flags: A or B|set a bit|build permission sets
emerald|XOR (^)|~1 if bits differ|toggle a bit|swap without a temp|find the unique number
violet|Shifts|~Move bits left/right|n << 1 doubles|n >> 1 halves|>>> fills with zero

sections.title: Practical Bitwise Operations Examples
Real-World Use Cases for Bitwise Operations
sections.content:
Use bitwise for **permission and flag systems** — file permissions (read=4, write=2, execute=1) combine into one number; `7` means all three (`4 | 2 | 1`). Check one with `(permissions & READ) != 0`.

Use it for **algorithm tricks** — `(n & (n - 1)) == 0` checks for a power of two, and XOR finds the single unique element in an array where everything else appears twice.

Use it in **networking** — IP addresses and subnet masks rely on bitwise AND.

As a backend developer you won't use these daily, but recognizing the flag pattern and the even/odd check signals low-level understanding.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing bitwise `&` with logical `&&`**: `if (x & y)` operates on bits, not boolean logic. Single `&` on integers is bit-level AND; `&&` is logical AND that short-circuits.
- **Not knowing any practical use**: memorizing operators but unable to name a use case. Be ready with permission flags or the even/odd check.
- **Forgetting precedence**: `if (flags & READ == 0)` parses as `flags & (READ == 0)` because equality binds tighter. Always use `if ((flags & READ) == 0)`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`&` (AND)** — outputs 1 only if both bits are 1; used to test if a bit is set.
- **`|` (OR)** — outputs 1 if either bit is 1; used to combine or set flags.
- **`^` (XOR)** — outputs 1 if bits differ; toggles bits and swaps values.
- **`~` (NOT)** — flips all bits; often combined with `&` to clear bits.
- **`<<` / `>>`** — shift bits to multiply/divide by powers of two.
- **Practical use** — permission masks, even/odd checks, and power-of-two operations.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of integer values, treating numbers as sequences of zeros and ones. There are seven main operators: ampersand for AND, pipe for OR, caret for XOR, tilde for NOT, double less-than for left shift, double greater-than for signed right shift, and triple greater-than for unsigned right shift. The most practical use I've seen is permission systems. Instead of storing multiple boolean fields for read, write, and execute permissions, you can pack them into a single integer using powers of two. For example, read equals 1, write equals 2, execute equals 4. To grant read and write, you use pipe: permissions equals READ pipe WRITE. To check if a user has read permission, you use ampersand: if permissions ampersand READ not equals zero. Another common use is checking if a number is even or odd. You can write n ampersand 1 equals zero to check if it's even, which is faster than using the modulo operator. Left shift is also useful: n shifted left by 1 multiplies n by 2, and shifting left by 3 multiplies by 8. One mistake freshers make is confusing bitwise ampersand with logical double ampersand. Single ampersand works on bits, double ampersand is for boolean logic. Another mistake is not knowing any real-world use case. If you can explain the permission flag pattern or the even-odd check, it shows you understand why these operators exist beyond theory.

questions.question: What is operator precedence in Java and what is a common pitfall with it?
questions.title: Operator Precedence in Java — Common Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: **Operator precedence** decides which operators run first in an expression without parentheses — `*` before `+`, relational before `&&`, and so on. The classic fresher trap is **string concatenation**: `"Result: " + 1 + 2` gives `"Result: 12"` (not `3`) because `+` is left-associative and the first `+` switches into String mode.

interviewer_intent.testing: Attention to evaluation order and the ability to predict expression outcomes, especially the string concatenation gotcha
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming all operators evaluate left-to-right uniformly, or not realizing string + numeric changes + behavior mid-expression
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the string concatenation precedence trap and show how parentheses fix it: "Result: " + (1 + 2) forces numeric addition first

sections.title: How Operator Precedence Controls Expression Evaluation
sections.content:
**Operator precedence** is Java's rule system that determines which operations happen first in an expression without parentheses, like math's order of operations: `2 + 3 * 4` equals 14, not 20.

The hierarchy: **unary** (`++`, `--`, `!`) is highest, then **multiplicative** (`*`, `/`, `%`), then **additive** (`+`, `-`), then **relational** (`>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`), then **equality** (`==`, `!=`), then **logical AND** (`&&`), then **logical OR** (`||`), and finally **assignment** (`=`) lowest. When operators share precedence, **associativity** decides order — most are left-associative, but assignment is right-associative.

The most insidious pitfall is **string concatenation**: `+` is overloaded for both addition and concatenation, and once one operand is a `String`, every subsequent `+` concatenates. So `"Result: " + 1 + 2` becomes `"Result: 12"`.

sections.title: Precedence Order at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Highest|~Unary first|++ -- and !|then * / %|then + and -
blue|Middle|~Comparisons next|relational < > <= >=|then == and !=|then logical AND
emerald|Lowest|~Logical then assign|logical OR|assignment =|= is right-associative
rose|Concat trap|~+ flips to String|"x" + 1 + 2 gives "x12"|left-to-right|wrap numbers in ( )

sections.title: Operator Precedence Pitfalls in Action
Wrong — the string concatenation trap
Right — parentheses force numeric addition
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **The string concatenation trap**: `"Total: " + num1 + num2` with `num1=3, num2=5` gives `"Total: 35"`, not `"Total: 8"`. Wrap numeric expressions: `"Total: " + (num1 + num2)`.
- **Assuming left-to-right for everything**: assignment is right-associative, so `a = b = 5` runs `b = 5` first.
- **Forgetting relational precedence**: `if (x > 0 && y > 0 == true)` parses unexpectedly because `==` binds differently than you expect. Group logical expressions with parentheses.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Hierarchy** — unary > multiplicative > additive > relational > equality > `&&` > `||` > assignment.
- **Associativity** — most operators are left-associative; assignment is right-associative.
- **Concatenation trap** — `"x" + 1 + 2` gives `"x12"`, not `"x3"`.
- **Parentheses override** — use them to force order and improve readability.
- **Relational before logical** — `x > 0 && y < 10` compares before the `&&`.
- **Clarity rule** — if order isn't obvious, add parentheses even if technically unnecessary.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Operator precedence determines which operations happen first when you have multiple operators in an expression without parentheses. It's like the order of operations in math: multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. So 2 plus 3 times 4 equals 14, not 20, because the multiplication happens first. Java has a full precedence hierarchy. Unary operators like plus plus and minus minus have the highest precedence, then multiplicative like star and slash, then additive like plus and minus, then relational like greater than and less than, then equality like double equals, then logical operators, and finally assignment has the lowest precedence. The classic pitfall that shows up in interviews is string concatenation with numbers. If you write quote Result colon quote plus 1 plus 2, you'd expect it to print Result colon 3, but it actually prints Result colon 1 2. Here's why: the first plus operator sees a string on the left and an integer on the right, so it converts 1 to a string and concatenates, giving you Result colon 1. Now the second plus sees a string on the left and 2 on the right, so it also concatenates, giving you Result colon 1 2. To fix this, you wrap the numeric part in parentheses: quote Result colon quote plus open paren 1 plus 2 close paren. The parentheses force numeric addition first, then concatenation. The lesson is, when in doubt, use parentheses. Even if the precedence rules technically make them unnecessary, parentheses make your intent clear and prevent these subtle bugs.
